settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The class is documented as a matcher only; whether a mismatch leads to an actual authorization bypass depends on how the surrounding filter chain and servlet container treat CR/LF, which is not visible in the read source.
No caller of RegexRequestMatcher and no configuration using it was read, so effective reachability of this code path in a real authorization decision is unverified.
candidates.description: RegexRequestMatcher.matches(HttpServletRequest) constructs the matched string as request.getServletPath(), then appends getPathInfo() if present and appends '?' + getQueryString() if present, and finally returns pattern.matcher(url).matches() (lines 91-113). There is no rejection of carriage-return/line-feed characters and no Pattern.DOTALL flag at compilation (lines 66-75 compile with only optional CASE_INSENSITIVE). Because in Java regex '.' does not match line terminators by default, a request path/query containing a raw \r or \n can cause a pattern of the common form (e.g. a prefix followed by '.*') to fail matching the constructed URL even though other servlet/application components may treat the same path as matching the protected pattern. This is the well-known authorization-bypass class for this class; the read source contains no CR/LF guard, so a bypass precondition exists where an application protects a path using RegexRequestMatcher with a pattern containing '.'.
missing_evidence: The tail of RegexRequestMatcher.java (lines 121-147, including the valueOf helper) was not read; it may contain additional handling.
No read of RequestMatcherDelegatingAuthorizationManager / FilterSecurityInterceptor / AntPathRequestMatcher to show how the match result is consumed.
No evidence in the snapshot that a container actually delivers CR/LF in servletPath/pathInfo.
preconditions: Application protects a path/pattern using RegexRequestMatcher (e.g. regexMatchers(...)) and the pattern relies on '.' wildcard semantics.
An attacker can cause a request for the protected path to carry a raw CR or LF in servletPath, pathInfo, or queryString (or a container that leaves such characters in those values).
A downstream component resolves/uses the same URI differently from how it is compared here, so the matched-vs-routed mismatch leads to reaching the protected resource.
candidates.title: RegexRequestMatcher matches request URL without rejecting CR/LF characters

counter_evidence: The read constructor and setters correctly populate and toggle the documented forbidden lists; nothing in the read span shows a removed check.
getFirewalledRequest's read body does call both rejectForbiddenHttpMethod and rejectedBlacklistedUrls, and additionally rejects non-normalized URLs and non-printable-ASCII requestURIs.
candidates.description: StrictHttpFirewall maintains two blacklists (encodedUrlBlacklist, decodedUrlBlacklist) and populates them in the constructor with FORBIDDEN_SEMICOLON, FORBIDDEN_FORWARDSLASH, FORBIDDEN_BACKSLASH plus ENCODED_PERCENT and FORBIDDEN_ENCODED_PERIOD on the encoded list and PERCENT on the decoded list (lines 79-107), with matching add/remove logic in the setters (lines 175-288). getFirewalledRequest() calls rejectForbiddenHttpMethod(request) and rejectedBlacklistedUrls(request), then rejects non-normalized URLs and non-printable-ASCII requestURIs before returning a FirewalledRequest (lines 290-308). The bodies of rejectedBlacklistedUrls(), isNormalized(), and containsOnlyPrintableAsciiCharacters() are outside the read span (the read portion ends at line 319; the file has 436 lines), so it cannot be verified from the inspected source whether the blacklists are checked against both the encoded and decoded URL, and whether the required checks are present and correctly applied. This is reported only as an unverified concern, not a confirmed vulnerability; the visible constructor and setter code appears consistent with the documented secure defaults (semicolon, encoded slash, backslash, encoded percent, encoded period all forbidden by default).
missing_evidence: Lines 320-436 of StrictHttpFirewall.java (rejectedBlacklistedUrls, isNormalized, containsOnlyPrintableAsciiCharacters, getFirewalledResponse) were not read.
No test file or caller of StrictHttpFirewall was read to confirm the default configuration is actually installed.
preconditions: A modified/weakened blacklist-check implementation in the unread part of the file would be required for an actual bypass.
An attacker-controlled request URL that relies on a forbidden pattern (e.g. encoded slash, backslash, semicolon, or double-encoded percent) to bypass a downstream URL-based security constraint.
candidates.title: StrictHttpFirewall URL blacklist enforcement not verifiable in read span (possible weakened firewall)

counter_evidence: The repositories are the project's documented/intended build repositories; snapshot plugin usage is explicit in the file.
No evidence of a compromised artifact, and gradle.properties pins springBootVersion=2.1.0.M4 and version=5.2.0.BUILD-SNAPSHOT.
candidates.description: build.gradle (lines 1-21) configures the buildscript block to fetch plugins from io.spring.gradle snapshot artifacts, an unversioned '-SNAPSHOT'/'-BUILD-SNAPSHOT' spring-build-conventions plugin, plus repositories including repo.spring.io/plugins-snapshot, plugins.gradle.org, repo.spring.io/plugins-release, a third-party https://dist.wso2.org/maven2, and mavenLocal(); subprojects also resolve artifacts from repo.maven.apache.org and repo.spring.io/libs-release (lines 47-53). Depending on mutable snapshot plugins and mavenLocal() can allow unexpected or locally shadowed artifacts to be used at build time. This is a build-supply-chain hygiene observation; no read source shows an exploitable dependency-confusion or malicious artifact, and gradle.properties (lines 1-3) only pins gaeVersion, springBootVersion, and the project version.
missing_evidence: No settings.gradle (read span) or repository policy/verification configuration was reviewed.
No evidence any build actually resolves from the third-party or snapshot repositories in a way that affects released artifacts.
preconditions: A developer or CI machine builds the project with these repositories enabled.
An attacker can publish to or influence the snapshot repositories or place artifacts in the local Maven cache.
candidates.title: Build script resolves plugins from remote snapshot repositories and mavenLocal()
